articles.title: Weekly Career Horoscope, September 27 to October 03, 2026: Success, challenges, and breakthroughs; Know about your Career
articles.summary: This week can bring more conversations than conclusions. A new client may approach you. Someone may suggest a collaboration.
articles.body: This week can bring more conversations than conclusions.A new client may approach you. Someone may suggest a collaboration. A senior could discuss a larger responsibility. An idea that looked casual a few weeks ago may suddenly start sounding commercially interesting.The temptation will be to say yes because the opportunity looks good.Don't. This week's career advantage comes from knowing which opportunity deserves your yes.AriesA partnership or collaboration can become professionally important. Someone may bring the network, skill or access you currently lack, but don't rush into an arrangement simply because the chemistry is good. Discuss responsibilities, money and expectations early. A promising partnership becomes valuable only when both people know what they are responsible for.TaurusYour workload may quietly expand. You could become the person everyone approaches because you are reliable, but additional work should not automatically become your responsibility. Look at your systems, delegate where possible and ask whether every meeting actually requires you. Being dependable should improve your career, not permanently overload your calendar.GeminiYour ability to present an idea becomes particularly useful. Writing, marketing, pitching, consulting, teaching and client-facing work can attract attention. A creative professional opportunity may also emerge. Don't dilute your energy by pursuing everything simultaneously. One idea presented exceptionally well can travel further than five ideas explained casually.CancerCareer decisions can feel unusually personal. You may become impatient with a role, senior or situation that no longer feels comfortable. Before making a dramatic move, separate temporary frustration from a genuine need for change. There is still room for professional expansion. Don't leave a good road simply because you encountered one difficult turn.LeoMoney and professional value come into focus. This can be a useful week to discuss compensation, pricing or the commercial side of your work. But don't walk into the conversation relying only on confidence. Bring results, numbers and examples. People may know you're good. Your job is to show them what being good has actually delivered.VirgoYour professional voice becomes stronger. Interviews, negotiations, presentations and important conversations can work in your favour, particularly when you keep the message simple. You don't need to explain every detail to prove that you've thought deeply. The smartest person in the room is often the one who can make the complicated sound clear.LibraThis is an important week for professional conversations. A client, collaborator or senior may become more receptive to your ideas, and negotiation becomes one of your strongest tools. But don't agree to unfavourable terms simply because you want the deal to happen. A good opportunity should still make sense after the excitement of getting it has disappeared.ScorpioSome of your most useful work can happen away from attention. Research, planning, strategy and preparing something for a later launch deserve time. An unfinished responsibility may also need closure before you move ahead. Don't announce every idea immediately. Some professional moves become stronger when they are built quietly first.SagittariusYour network can open a door. A former colleague, friend, client or professional community may introduce an opportunity you would not have found independently. Attend the useful conversation, but don't confuse networking with collecting contacts. You don't need another hundred people who know your name. You need a few who understand what you actually do.CapricornVisibility can increase, bringing both opportunity and responsibility. A senior may notice your work or you may be asked to take ownership of something important. Accept growth, but understand what comes with it before saying yes. A bigger title is valuable only when the responsibility, authority and reward make sense together.AquariusSomething beyond your existing professional world may become interesting. A new technology, course, international opportunity, research area or completely different business direction can catch your attention. Explore it seriously without immediately abandoning what already works. You can investigate the next chapter without prematurely closing the current one.PiscesMoney, responsibility and professional boundaries may become interconnected. Be careful about vague arrangements involving commissions, shared projects or somebody expecting you to contribute more than originally discussed. Put important terms in writing. Professional trust becomes stronger when nobody has to rely on memory for what was agreed.Career Message of the WeekBefore accepting the project, collaboration, responsibility or meeting, ask:Does this improve my career?Does it deserve my time?Is the return worth the responsibility?And what will I have to say no to if I say yes to this?Career growth isn't always about adding another opportunity.Sometimes it comes from becoming selective enough to recognise which opportunity actually deserves you.This article is written by, Sidhharrth S Kumaar, Registered Pharmacist, Astro Numerologist, Life & Relationship Coach, Vaastu Expert, IKS Expert, I Ching Expert, Energy Healer, Music Therapist, Author of “Think like a Sage Lead like a CEO” series and Chief Astro Strategy Officer (CASO), NumroVani.Get the latest astrology news and horoscope updates. articles.title: Amit Shah flags off India's first LNG train in Gujarat, launches Rs 1,542 crore railway projects
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Union home and cooperation minister Amit Shah on Sunday flagged off India’s first LNG-powered train in Gujarat and launched a series of railway
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Union home and cooperation minister Amit Shah on Sunday flagged off India’s first LNG-powered train in Gujarat and launched a series of railway projects worth more than Rs 1,542 crore at Sabarmati.The LNG-based train uses a diesel-LNG dual-fuel system, with two 1,400 HP Driving Power Cars at the Sabarmati Integrated Coaching Depot converted to run on both fuels. LNG can replace nearly 40 per cent of diesel consumption under the system.The initiative is aimed at reducing diesel use and fuel costs while lowering emissions including carbon dioxide, nitrogen oxides and particulate matter.The train was among several railway projects launched by Shah in Sabarmati, with the package also focusing on railway safety, line capacity and freight operations.Shah also laid the foundation stone for the indigenous Kavach automatic train protection system across 404 km of railway network in the Ahmedabad division.The project, estimated to cost around Rs 411 crore, covers 157 km of the Ahmedabad-Palanpur section and 247 km of the Ahmedabad-Samakhiyali section. Kavach is designed to help prevent train collisions, protect against overspeeding and reduce risks linked to human error.An automatic block signalling system has also been introduced across 122.57 km of railway sections between Sabarmati-Kalol-Bhandu Motidau and Sabarmati-Sanand-Jakhwada at a cost of around Rs 118.83 crore. The system is designed to maintain safe distances between trains and increase route capacity.Shah also inaugurated the WAG-12 locomotive maintenance shed at Sabarmati, built at an estimated cost of Rs 700 crore.The facility will provide maintenance for 300 high-horsepower WAG-12 electric locomotives, which have a capacity of around 12,000 HP and are designed to haul heavy and long freight trains.The Sabarmati-Sarkhej railway line doubling project, estimated at Rs 313.27 crore, will cover a 21-km stretch and is targeted for completion by March 2028.The project covers stations including Sabarmati, Gandhigram, Vastrapur and Sarkhej and includes bridges and road underpasses.The doubling is expected to improve train movement and connectivity towards the Sarkhej-Dholera region while supporting industrial and commercial activity in the area.The projects launched in Gujarat are aimed at improving railway safety, increasing operational capacity and promoting alternative-fuel technology in rail transport.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1933, a secret giver mailed $5 checks to struggling families; 75 years later, his grandson opened an attic suitcase holding thank-you letters
articles.summary: Discover the inspiring story of Samuel J. Stone, a secret benefactor during the Great Depression, whose generosity impacted 150 families. Uncovered by his granddaughter, this tale reveals the profound effects of a hidden act of kindness.
articles.body: In December 1933, at the depth of the Great Depression, a small advertisement appeared in the Canton Repository, a local newspaper in Canton, Ohio. Titled "In Consideration of the White Collar Man!", it was signed only by "B. Virdot" and promised financial help to families willing to write in and describe their hardship. The anonymous donor was Canton business owner Samuel J. Stone, who owned a menswear shop with his wife, Minna, and originally intended to send each of the seventy-five families ten dollars. So many letters of desperation arrived that he changed his mind and ended up giving five dollars to each of 150 families. He sent each of these donations via checks written at the same local bank and signed using the fake name he had created using the first names of all three of his daughters, Barbara, Virginia and Dorothy. The identity of Stone was kept anonymous and his secret remained hidden for seventy-five years until its revelation in June 2008. The secret was revealed by his grandson, writer Ted Gup, when he visited his mother for her eightieth birthday and took home with him an old suitcase filled with documents she thought he might be interested in looking at. He did not open the suitcase for months, but when he did, he found a bunch of tattered letters and bank statements dated December 1933.How the suitcase came to hold a stranger's secretA review of the resulting book, published in a University of Minnesota library journal, describes how Gup pieced the mystery together only after finding the original Canton Repository clipping among the suitcase's contents, which named an anonymous donor signing as B. Virdot. A conversation with his mother verified through the paperwork that his grandfather had advertised and was sending five-dollar checks anonymously to families in the community who were suffering from the economic hardships of the Depression. It is mentioned in the review that while Sam and Minna Stone were not rich by today's standards, in the year 1933 they were prosperous enough to be able to run their own business, feed their children and have little luxuries when compared to many of their neighbors. In between the appeals for help were the checks themselves, cancelled and returned to Stone's own account after the families had cashed them, still bearing the signature of B. Virdot, along with thank-you letters from families to whom the money had been sent and who wanted to let this stranger know how much the help had meant to them.Why the discovery reached far beyond one family's atticMoreover, according to the University of Minnesota review, as Gup delved deeper into the history of the items in the case, he was led into the exploration of his grandfather's whole life story, discovering the truth that Sam Stone was not originally from America but was from Romania, where he was known as Samuel Finkelstein. The book that resulted, titled A Secret Gift, was later selected for the State Library of Ohio's Choose to Read Ohio program, which encourages public libraries and schools across the state to build community readership around Ohio authors. In the materials from that program, there is a record that after the story about Stone's secret generosity became known, the same idea was revived locally when community members modified the original $5 gift according to inflation rates to $100, and once again invited the Canton families to write in with their stories about their needs, repeating the exact thing that Stone had done secretly in 1933.In addition, the University of Minnesota review emphasizes the fact that the letters found in the suitcase revealed not only material difficulties. There were letters from some of the recipients explaining that they were keeping children from needy families because those families could not afford to provide for them, or postponing their layoffs in order to keep the business running as long as possible.What one suitcase revealed about a hidden act of generosityThe importance of the story does not lie in how much was at stake, but rather in the fact that Stone had never taken any of the credit for it all. He invented an entire new identity, just to make sure that those whom he helped could never give him the recognition he deserved. In order to find out who had helped his family, Gup had to discover a forgotten suitcase that had belonged to Stone's own family. For Gup, opening the suitcase was about more than solving the mystery within his own family; it was also about bringing to light the actions of a mysterious man who had quietly helped so many of his struggling neighbors during their toughest winter.You use AI every day. articles.title: Israel’s Netanyahu criticises opposition uniting against him for elections
articles.summary: Five opposition leaders agree to cooperate to boost voter turnout to secure a majority in the October 27 elections.
articles.body:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has criticised the opposition leaders who began coordinating to replace his government ahead of the October 27 Knesset elections.

The five politicians met at opposition leader Yair Lapid’s home in Tel Aviv on Saturday to coordinate their strategy before the elections, Israel’s Channel 12 reported.

In his first response to the agreement, Netanyahu claimed Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot would seek to form a government with Yair Lapid, Yair Golan, Bennett 2026, Yisrael Beiteinu and Arab parties.

“Only a strong Likud will stop them,” Netanyahu posted on X, referring to his right-wing political party. He posted an AI-altered photo of the politicians meeting where he added United Arab List leader Mansour Abbas and Hadash-Ta’al leader Ahmad Tibi.

The meeting was attended by Lapid, the leader of Yesh Atid; Naftali Bennett, the leader of Bennett 2026; Avigdor Lieberman, the head of Yisrael Beiteinu; Gadi Eisenkot, the head of Yashar; and Democrats leader Yair Golan.

Lapid posted a group picture and a document listing their principles for coordination until the election and afterwards.

Under the document, each party leader pledged to work within their respective constituencies to boost voter turnout and attract support from various sectors of society, to secure a majority and form a new government.

The document also says three joint working groups are to be established within 48 hours.

The first will focus on boosting voter turnout for the bloc and what the opposition leaders described as “safeguarding the integrity of the election”. A second group will draft the basic guidelines of the government the opposition seeks to form, including establishing an official commission of inquiry into the attacks of October 7, 2023, and drafting a new constitution. The third group will coordinate media activity and try to counter what the document described as “fake news and smear campaigns”.

“I am filled with hope again tonight. I am confident that we can win 63 seats and work together to fix Israel,” Bennett, a former prime minister, said in a statement on X.

“We have agreed to fully cooperate until the election, on election day, and after the election, with the aim of forming a government that will fix Israel,” he added.

articles.title: Photos: Pope Leo draws hundreds of thousands for open-air Mass in Paris
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV celebrates an open-air mass for hundreds of thousands of believers on the Champs-Elysees.
articles.body:
Hundreds of thousands of people packed Paris’s iconic Champs-Elysees to attend an open-air Mass led by Pope Leo XIV.

The Vatican said about 800,000 people were at the service on Saturday – roughly 200,000 more than those who had registered in advance.

The pope greeted flag-waving, cheering crowds from his popemobile during a 2km (1.2-mile) parade along the grand boulevard leading to Place de la Concorde.

An imposing stage built for the mass, topped with a golden cross, and row upon row of choir singers, clergy and worshippers praying under the pope’s gaze on Place de la Concorde marked a new chapter for the history-steeped square that was an execution site during the French Revolution. Louis XVI and Marie-Antoinette were guillotined there. For many in France, it embodies the republic and traditionally stages Bastille Day celebrations.

Organisers say it is the only site in central Paris able to hold such large crowds.

But the choice of location has drawn criticism from supporters of France’s strict secularism in public life, rooted in a 1905 law separating church and state. They argue that Place de la Concorde symbolises the republic, and that other venues, such as Les Invalides, the complex where Pope Benedict XVI celebrated mass with 240,000 people in 2008, would have been more appropriate.

articles.title: Two mass shootings in South Africa leave 27 dead
articles.summary: The two attacks hours apart come as the country struggles to stop high levels of gang-related armed violence.
articles.body:
Twenty-seven people have been killed in two mass shootings hours apart in South Africa, the latest gun violence to hit the country.

Seventeen people were killed when eight gunmen stormed a bar close to Johannesburg on Saturday evening, with 15 more injured.

In a separate shooting in the early hours of Sunday morning, 10 people were killed outside an entertainment venue in a township near Cape Town and a further 11 were injured.

South Africa has one of the highest murder rates in the world and has struggled to contain gang-related gun violence in recent years. Police have not given a definitive motive for either of the latest attacks.

In Johannesburg, gunmen opened fire on customers outside the bar before continuing the attack inside and torching two vehicles before fleeing.

Police said thirteen men and four women were killed.

Gauteng Police Commissioner Lt Gen Tommy Mthombeni said people from Ethiopia and Lesotho were among those caught up in the shooting, but that the vast majority were South African.

He also said police believed the motive behind the shooting was robbery, as personal belongings had been taken, but that they could not rule out turf wars between illegal mining groups.

Earlier, deputy provincial police commissioner Maj Gen Fred Kekana said the attack may have been a retaliation for an incident last month, in which one person was killed and another wounded, according to news agency AFP.

He said at the scene that police had clear pictures and in some cases names for the suspects.

In Cape Town, five victims died at the scene and a further five people died in hospital.

No arrests had been made in either case on Sunday morning.

The two mass shootings came days after 11 people were killed in the city of Durban when gunmen stormed a house in the KwaMakhutha township.

Illegal weapons are prevalent in South Africa and gun violence has been a persistent problem for decades, with about 60 murders recorded every day in the country of 62 million.

But a recent spate of mass shootings has raised fears that the problem is deepening, with violence often linked to turf wars between gangs engaged in drug trafficking and illegal mining.

In February, President Cyril Ramaphosa called organised crime "the most immediate threat to our democracy, our society and our economic development".

Earlier this year, the military was deployed alongside police in areas with the highest murder rates in an effort to reduce armed violence.

On Saturday, a tenth woman's body was found in Ekurhuleni , to the east of Johannesburg, with local police saying they were unable to rule out a serial killer operating in the area with similarities between the deaths.

articles.title: Before BTS and Blackpink, there was Big Bang: Now the 'Kings of K-pop' are back
articles.summary: Big Bang played London's Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, marking a long-awaited return for the group that helped build the blueprint for modern K-pop.
articles.body:
A sea of glowing yellow crowns. Thousands of voices chanting in Korean.

An explosive surge of energy as the opening synth riffs of Fantastic Baby shatter the stadium air. Big Bang is back.

Fourteen years after their first major European shows, and after a decade marked by military service, member departures and legal scandals, the South Korean group played at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London on Saturday as part of their 20th anniversary world tour.

Inside the near-capacity venue, the crowd did not just watch a concert - they stepped into a significant moment in K-pop history.

As the band emerged in their trademark high-fashion, glittering outfits, the crowd danced freely, setting the tone for an evening that felt less like a routine tour stop and more like a homecoming.

For fans, it is a long-awaited reunion. But the significance of Big Bang's return extends beyond nostalgia.

Years before BTS were selling out Wembley Stadium and Blackpink were headlining Hyde Park, Big Bang were already proving Korean pop could succeed far beyond Asia.

The group filled arenas across the West, collaborated with major American artists, experimented with hip-hop and electronic music, and turned their own fashion and creative identities into part of their appeal.

Having attended their European debut at Wembley Arena in 2012, the shift in atmosphere on Saturday was striking.

Where their original UK shows were driven by a hunger to prove themselves and promote a new album, this return as a trio, comprising G-Dragon, Taeyang and Daesung, felt entirely crafted for their dedicated community.

By reworking classic tracks and cleverly remixing songs to accommodate absent members, the group relied on pyrotechnics, their signature live band and sheer stage presence rather than elaborate staging.

The result was a reunion that felt celebratory, grounded and playful.

In 2011, Big Bang became the first K-pop group to win a major Western music award when they took home the newly created Worldwide Act prize at the MTV Europe Music Awards.

When they made their European debut at Wembley Arena in December 2012, a second show was added after the first sold out in under two hours.

They were leading a pioneering generation that proved global crossover was genuinely possible.

Then in 2016, Forbes estimated Big Bang had earned $44m (£33.2m) over the previous year, making them the first K-pop act to appear on its Celebrity 100 List.

"When it comes to the global market for K-pop, there is no doubt Big Bang made a huge contribution," says Dr Haekyung Um, senior lecturer in music at the University of Liverpool.

"Earlier acts were popular within Asian markets, but Big Bang were true international stars. I would call them the Kings of K-pop, just as we call Michael Jackson the King of Pop," Um adds.

"Big Bang's success really was an early signal of how successful a K-pop stadium tour in the West could truly be."

Before Big Bang, K-pop groups were often viewed as heavily manufactured by entertainment agencies.

But music critics say Big Bang broke the mould. They wrote and produced their own songs, shaped their own streetwear image and blended genres ranging from hip-hop and R&B to trot, a traditional South Korean folk genre.

For many attending on Saturday, the show served as a direct lesson in K-pop's lineage - a chance to see "the idols' idols" perform live.

"They were different because they didn't follow the uniform K-pop cookie-cutter pretty boy phase," explains Sharon, who was visiting London from Singapore.

"They went harder on their music, a bit more hip-hop. They did what they had to do, and they are the absolute OGs for me."

The shift set them apart across Asia and helped establish the blueprint for modern self-produced acts such as BTS.

And then there is the yellow crown. At Big Bang concerts, it is impossible to miss the group's crown-shaped lightstick, known as the Bang Bong.

In early K-pop, fans supported artists by waving coloured balloons or generic glow sticks.

But seeking a distinct, permanent identity for their fandom, dubbed "VIPs", band leader G-Dragon proposed a handheld yellow crown, setting the template for custom concert merchandise.

"Fan engagement and coordinated chants have deep roots in Korean music history," explains Um. "But Big Bang helped modernise the physical technology."

The Bang Bong established a model for custom-designed fandom lightsticks and merchandise that modern K-pop groups now follow.

Outside the venue, that same fan-led energy spilled into the streets, with attendees trading handmade gifts and photo cards - a ritual that has spread to Western arena tours in recent years.

Volunteer fan groups distributed roughly 35,000 custom-printed banners across the stadium, co-ordinating a massive crowd-wide salute to be raised in unison during select performances.

Big Bang's story, however, is far from a straightforward tale of success.

South Korea requires able-bodied men to complete mandatory military service, and Big Bang's members served at different points during the group's hiatus.

In 2017, former band member T.O.P was convicted of marijuana use, an offence heavily criminalised and socially taboo in South Korea, and received a suspended prison sentence while serving his mandatory military duty. He later formally departed from the group.

Then in 2019, the group's youngest member, Seungri, permanently retired from entertainment amid the "Burning Sun" scandal.

It was a high-profile police investigation into a Seoul nightclub of the same name which exposed a network of sex trafficking, bribery, and illicit filming involving several male K-pop stars.

South Korea's Supreme Court later upheld an 18-month prison sentence for Seungri in 2022 on charges including prostitution mediation, overseas gambling, and embezzlement.

Although the band didn't openly acknowledge the departure of two of their former members from the stage, their absence was obvious to long-time fans in the audience.

Though it did not matter to fans like Annie, who flew from New York to see the show with friends. She said Big Bang's perseverance through hardship made their music mean even more.

"Big Bang was my starter," she says. "I love how they move through the obstacles - it gives me hope. After years of hiatus, it's amazing they're coming back. They are the OGs."

The crowd erupted as the opening chant of Bang Bang Bang echoed before the band even walked out, while their iconic 2008 ballad Haru Haru produced a massive stadium-wide singalong.

The K-pop industry Big Bang helped build has changed almost beyond recognition.

Yet their return has drawn a striking mix of original second-generation fans and younger Gen Z listeners who were barely born when the group debuted.

While many veteran followers grew up alongside the band, a whole new generation discovered them through digital archives or cross-media appearances.

Gemma and her daughter Casey travelled from Edinburgh wearing handmade custom jackets.

"I found out about them through T.O.P in Squid Game and then fell down a rabbit hole," Gemma says. "I've converted so many of my friends to K-pop now. It's all about the energy."

For Korean diaspora fans, the show carried an even deeper cultural resonance.

"I got into Big Bang when their Alive EP (in 2012) was released because I felt they were quite ground-breaking," says Kevin.

"Before, I felt there was a lot of mimicking by Korean artists on what was happening in the West, but here they took full ownership of their unique identity. It's very rare in K-pop that you have a band around for 20 years, and they definitely played a part in making K-pop mainstream."

Much of this multi-generational pull is driven by archival concert footage, TV appearances, and classic music videos circulating across social media platforms like TikTok and YouTube.

"Nostalgia can be built upon something people didn't even experience personally at the time," notes Um.

"It comes through shared digital memory. YG Entertainment was early in leveraging digital platforms like YouTube, which built a lasting global fan foundation that has accumulated across two generations."

While the band refrained from directly addressing their past on stage, the emotional weight of their history peaked during the finale Still Life.

As T.O.P's unmistakable baritone echoed through the stadium via recorded vocals, a visible wave of emotion swept across the crowd.

Addressing the venue during the encore, G-Dragon appeared clearly moved, admitting they never expected their music to leave such an enduring global mark 14 years after their London debut.

As fireworks lit up the night sky, the three members linked hands and bowed deeply - a triumphant moment for the group widely credited with helping reshape modern K-pop.

articles.title: UK police evacuate homes near RAF Fairford airbase used by US
articles.summary: Police say they have arrested several men on suspicion of explosives-related offences.
articles.body:
Police have evacuated homes near an airbase in the United Kingdom used by the United States military and arrested several men on suspicion of explosives-related offences.

“The army’s specialist explosive ordnance disposal team are currently ⁠examining a number of vehicles,” Gloucestershire police said on Sunday, adding that “a major incident” had been declared.

Residents from a number of properties in Whelford, southwestern England, were being taken to a nearby leisure centre. Police said several men had been arrested “on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act”.

The town is located near RAF Fairford, an airbase that US forces have used for strikes during the US-Israel war on Iran.

A reporter from the Reuters news agency at the scene said armed police had blocked access to the base’s main gate, while equipment had been placed in front of entry points.

About 30 emergency vehicles, including police cars, ambulances and fire engines, were stationed in the nearby town of Fairford.

Gloucestershire police said in a statement they would like “to reassure people that we believe this incident is contained”.

Britain’s Defence Secretary Wes Streeting thanked the emergency and specialist teams who responded to the incident.

“We can be reassured that this is being dealt with,” he said.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham is receiving updates on the situation, his office said. Local media said counter-terrorism police were leading the investigation.

There was no immediate information about what prompted the arrests, whether explosives were found, or if the suspected offences were connected to the airbase.

The US Air Force said it was aware of reports about the incident but declined to discuss specific security measures.

A spokesperson said the 501st Combat Support Wing, a US Air Force unit in Britain, and other US units based in the UK remained vigilant and would take steps needed to protect personnel and their families.

In March, three US B-1B Lancer bombers touched down at RAF Fairford after what is believed to be the first US strike mission against Iran launched from a British base, during the war on Iran.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, a powerful military force that operates alongside the country’s regular armed forces, warned in July that bases used to launch attacks on Iran could be treated as legitimate targets.

Authorities have not linked Sunday’s arrests to Iran or said RAF Fairford was a target.

articles.title: How an American teacher’s $5,000 donation helped turn a Chinese desert into a lush, green forest
articles.summary: HONG KONG — Ronald Sakolsky never thought his money would go this far.
articles.body: HONG KONG — Ronald Sakolsky never thought his money would go this far. What was once a vast, dry desert in northern China has transformed into a lush, green forest of 50,000 full-grown trees, thanks in part to a $5,000 donation he made more than a quarter century ago to a local farmer and “sand-control worker” named Yin Yuzhen. Sakolsky, 69, a retired teacher from Pennsylvania, was amazed to see the transformation in China’s Inner Mongolia region last month when he visited for the first time in 26 years. “Seeing it with my own eyes, that was the biggest surprise,” he told Chinese state media. “I saw pictures, I was told all about it, but until you see it is when you realize that it’s real.” Sakolsky and Yin’s reunion last month has been held up by Chinese authorities as an example of how China and the United States, the world’s two biggest greenhouse gas emitters, can work together on global issues such as climate change. Chinese leader Xi Jinping, in Washington this week for a summit with President Donald Trump, mentioned Sakolsky’s story in his toast at a state dinner on Thursday, saying it “touches the hearts of many Chinese people and stands as a shining example of the friendly exchanges between our two peoples.” Sakolsky was teaching English on exchange in China’s central Henan province in 1999 when he saw a TV news report about Yin. More than a decade earlier, the newly married Yin had started planting trees as a way to feel less isolated in her new home in the Mu Us Desert, also known as the Maowusu Desert (“bad water” in Mongolian). Moved by her story, Sakolsky raised $5,000, which was many times Yin’s annual income, so she could plant even more. They met in person in 2000, when Yin promised Sakolsky that she and her family would take good care of the saplings. Earlier this year, Yin launched an online campaign to track down Sakolsky, and last month he made a 10-day visit to China that included an emotional reunion with Yin in her forest, where the trees now stand more than 30 feet high and the government has named a grove after him. The two of them planted a friendship tree, and Sakolsky collected a jar of sand to take home to Pennsylvania. Yin also gave him a cross-stitch with the words “One Earth, One Dream.” “I want him to know that I kept my word, and that Chinese people keep our promises,” she said. Yin called Sakolsky her “brother” and said the sapling they planted together would be standing tall in another 26 years. Reports on Sakolsky’s visit have been heavily promoted by Chinese authorities and widely viewed on Chinese social media, where commenters described him as “a real friend of Chinese people.” Tree-planting efforts are part of a decadeslong government campaign sometimes referred to as China’s “Great Green Wall,” which was launched in 1978 as a 73-year effort intended to reduce sandstorms and help stave off desertification associated with global climate change. Away from emotional stories like Yin’s, the campaign has had mixed success. While the Great Green Wall is a “great initiative in principle,” the Chinese government tends to emphasize “top-down, technocratic solutions to environmental problems” and focus on targets more than quality, said Judith Shapiro, who teaches at American University in the department of environment, development and health. The loss of open land for nomadic herding as a result of the initiative “remains a serious blow to some ethnic minority nationalities,” she said. In the program’s early years, deserts were lined with “fast-growing but water-hungry” trees such as poplars that depleted water tables, though more suitable and biodiverse species are now being planted. “Overall, the Chinese government has done a good job instilling the idea that trees are a great benefit to society,” Shapiro said. The climate connection Days after Sakolsky met with Yin in China’s arid north, a likely impact of the changing climate was felt when a devastating flood struck 2,000 miles away along the Nepal-China border. More than 1,400 people have been confirmed dead and thousands remain missing across Nepal and China’s Tibet region after the Aug. 26 disaster, which experts say was linked to warming temperatures in the Himalayas. “I am very, very sad for the people in Nepal and people in China,” Sakolsky said at a news conference in Beijing on Aug. 31. “I know now the world is alive, and if I keep throwing paper on the ground or if I keep letting trees die, I am killing the life of the world, which means I am actually killing mankind.” The Tibet flood was one of several disasters this summer in China, where flooding triggered by Tropical Storm Maysak in early July killed at least 159 people in the southern region of Guangxi. At least 16 people in Jiangxi province were killed in a Sept. 5 mudslide set off by torrential rain linked to Typhoon Saudel. Researchers said last year that climate change is making such storms in Asia more frequent and severe. China says it plans to reach peak carbon emissions before 2030 and achieve carbon neutrality by 2060. Its carbon emissions have been “flat or falling” since 2024 and are on track to fall in 2026 for the second year in a row, according to an analysis for Carbon Brief this month by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air. While its coal emissions are still rising, China is seeking to fill a void in global climate leadership left by the U.S., the world’s largest carbon emitter historically, which withdrew from the Paris climate agreement during Trump’s first days back in office last year. Critics say China’s goals are too cautious and will leave it unable to meet its Paris Agreement pledge to cut emissions by 65% from 2005 to 2030. Trump and Xi were not expected to have any meaningful discussion about climate change at their summit this week. Sakolsky said last month that both countries have common interests, including combating climate change. “You want the best for your children because you know they are tomorrow,” he said. “You want the best for your country, but it does not mean you have to sacrifice your children.” Sakolsky called on anyone inspired by his friendship with Yin to “go out and plant one tree.” “If everybody plants one tree in their backyard or in their park after watching this,” he said, “can you imagine how many trees we would have in the world?” Jennifer Jett reported from Hong Kong, and Erin Tan and Fred Dufour from Beijing.

articles.title: Bomb squad searching vans near U.S. air base in Britain as five men arrested on terror charge
articles.summary: LONDON — British police arrested several men on suspicion of terror and explosives offenses on Sunday and evacuated homes near an air base that the U.S.
articles.body: LONDON — British police arrested several men on suspicion of terror and explosives offenses on Sunday and evacuated homes near an air base that the U.S. Air Force had been using to facilitate strikes on Iran. A major incident was declared, with a massive emergency presence seen around RAF Fairford, which is about 90 minutes outside London, close to the village of Whelford in west England. The Gloucestershire police force said it responded in the early hours of Sunday to reports of three suspicious vehicles moving toward the base, and arrested five men “on suspicion of committing offenses under the Explosives Act.” They were later further arrested on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act. Police did not provide further details on the men, who remain in custody, or what they were suspected to have done. “Work to establish the full nature of this incident is ongoing,” a police spokesperson said. The force said 85 homes across the local area were evacuated and a 440-yard cordon put in place while an Army ordnance disposal team examines the vehicles. Helicopter footage from Sky News showed multiple white vans close to the base seemingly being searched by a bomb disposal robot. Julian Tudsbery, who has lived in Whelford for 30 years, told Britain’s Press Association another resident had reported three suspicious vans in the village. Along with other residents, Tudsbery has since been evacuated to a nearby recreation center. The Reuters news agency had reported that security measures at the air ‌base have been significantly increased in recent ‌days. A spokesperson for the U.S. ‌Air Force told the agency they would not discuss specific force protection measures. “The 501st Combat Support Wing and our fellow ⁠UK-based Wings remain vigilant and ⁠will take appropriate actions to ensure the safety and security ‌of our US service members, civilians, contractors, and their families,” the spokesperson ‌said, ahead of the police statement. “We constantly assess ⁠a variety of factors that determine what measures we institute or modify to protect our installations, our people and their families,” they added. The British government said Prime Minister Andy Burnham is being updated about the incident, adding “it would be inappropriate to comment further whilst investigations are ongoing.” In March this year, Burnham’s predecessor Keir Starmer gave permission for the U.S. to use its bases for “specific and limited defensive” operations against Iran. In July, Iran’s ⁠Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps warned Britain that “any base used to invade Iranian territory is our legitimate target,” Iran’s semiofficial Tasnim news agency reported, citing bomber aircraft flights from Fairford. At the time, a British government spokesperson said that the country was “ready to keep the United Kingdom safe from any kind of attacks, whether it’s on our soil or from abroad.” Roz Savage, the local member of Parliament, thanked police for their response to “worrying scenes just outside the RAF Fairford base,” while British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said in a post on X: “We can be reassured that this is being dealt with and it is exactly why our emergency response teams and Armed Forces are on standby 24/7.”

articles.title: Russia intensifies hybrid war beyond Ukraine, rattling Europe
articles.summary: European leaders are raising alarm that Russia is intensifying its years-long hybrid war against NATO member states, lashing out as it struggles to make decisive gains in its nearly five-year war against Ukraine. Officials say the attacks against European countries include sabotage against infrastructure, targeted violence against political opponents or perceived enemies, and hostile influence…
articles.body:
European leaders are raising alarm that Russia is intensifying its years-long hybrid war against NATO member states, lashing out as it struggles to make decisive gains in its nearly five-year war against Ukraine.

Officials say the attacks against European countries include sabotage against infrastructure, targeted violence against political opponents or perceived enemies, and hostile influence operations ranging from bribery, election interference to disinformation campaigns.

In the U.S., members of Russia’s intelligence service plotted assassinations of political dissidents and Ukraine supporters, according to details recently revealed in an indictment by the Department of Justice. The accused remain at large.

“It’s full scale,” Latvia’s Foreign Minister Baiba Braže said in an interview with The Hill.

She described Russia’s actions as a subconventional war against Europe and the U.S. — moving beyond what’s been described as the Kremlin’s “hybrid” or “gray zone” warfare against NATO.

“Those activities cannot be called hybrid anymore because they are actual attacks,” she said.

The public awareness campaign is a key element of Europe’s counterresponse, working to fortify its defenses against such attacks without escalating into a kinetic war with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Of the three Baltic states, Latvia has the distinction of combating hybrid warfare on two borders, both Russia and Belarus. Braže described suspected acts of Russian sabotage in the country as arson on munition factories and warehouses storing arms for Ukraine. And Belarus’s authoritarian president, Alexander Lukashenko, has weaponized migration to put pressure on Baltic borders. In August, Latvian authorities said they discovered a tunnel used by migrants to cross over from Belarus.

“It’s an organized migrant activity against the external border of NATO and the EU,” Braže said, describing it as a scheme run by Belarus’s security forces and with ties to Russia.

Another key part of Europe’s defense against Russia is increasing support for Ukraine. This includes weapons, but also the financial backing to support its war-battered economy, and sanctioning and isolating Russian businesses and officials supporting Putin’s war.

President Trump has taken a different track, reaching out to Putin with flattery and reportedly offering economic partnerships without demanding a ceasefire or war-end. Trump earlier this month signed into law a bill that allows him to tariff countries doing the most trade with Russia, but it’s unclear when he might use it.

Braže warned against any economic partnership in Putin’s Russia, where companies face the risk of having their businesses confiscated, nationalized or even punished criminally.

“Currently it’s very difficult to imagine an economy in Russia that is not controlled by this authoritarian regime,” she said. “There is no free economy, so it’s a risk for any entrepreneur, for any company working in Russia.”

Increased vigilance on defending Europe’s borders and critical infrastructure is the priority strategy in combating Russia’s hybrid threats for countries in the region.

Other measures include expelling Russian diplomats suspected of being spies; limiting the entry of Russian nationals to Europe; increasing cooperation among European security services to share information about suspected Russian sabotage; and bolstering security around vulnerable targets, including national infrastructure, military production facilities and even high-profile people.

One option that’s generally not discussed publicly is hitting Russia back with more conventional military action.

That could escalate to full-blown war, cautioned Elisabeth Braw, a senior fellow with the Atlantic Council, who focuses on defense against gray-zone and hybrid threats.

“It’s important to remember that even though lots of social media users and the armchair generals say we should hit back strongly, powerfully, if we escalated, if we responded with military means to these attacks, then Russia would respond with military means,” she said.

“And we would have war. And surely that can’t be in our interest.”

In the realm of deterrence, CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s August visit with intelligence counterparts in Moscow was in part to warn Russia against escalating sabotage operations in Europe, Reuters reported , citing two people familiar with the matter.

Following the high-profile visit, the Baltic capitals, in particular, have downplayed a conventional Russian military threat, an attempt to lower the temperature, even as officials call out the increasing Russian hybrid warfare.

“I want to emphasize that, at present, Estonia’s military threat assessment remains unchanged,” Estonia’s Minister of Defense Martin Herem posted Wednesday on the social platform X.

He was responding to Denmark’s intelligence assessment released that day raising the possibility Russia could launch a limited military attack against one or several NATO countries bordering Russia.

The assessment also warned that Russia’s escalating hybrid warfare could “include destructive cyber attacks that cripple critical societal functions as well as sabotage attacks that carry a high risk of casualties.”

“Our security authorities have repeatedly succeeded in identifying those responsible for similar attacks and have also prevented a number of attacks before they could take place,” he wrote. “At present, neither Estonia, Denmark nor our other NATO Allies see a threat that would require raising the readiness of the armed forces.”

Braw backs the defensive measures. In her upcoming book, “Undersea War,” she tracks how increased NATO naval patrols in the Baltic Sea have helped halt what had become escalating instances of damage to subsea cables and pipelines — a critical global network powering internet and electric connectivity.

“We’ve had decades of subsea cables and pipelines, and there has only been occasional damage, every so often,” she said.

But over the past five years, “mysterious and very severe incidents involving subsea cables” have increased, she explained, in the Baltic Sea and around Taiwan — which is on the front lines of Chinese aggression.

“That is part of the larger picture that we are seeing in Europe, that Russia is using,” she said.

Earlier this year, the United Kingdom and Norway deployed military vessels to disperse Russian submarines operating near sensitive subsea cables and pipelines. Reuters reported this month that the Russian subs were training with a secret weapon designed to disable undersea cables without leaving any fingerprints, citing two Western officials.

Braw acknowledged Russia’s innovation, but she also pointed to the fact that hybrid or gray zone warfare operations “are not difficult to carry out,” especially with sabotage acts that don’t require high-level training, such as placing explosives at railways or starting fires at warehouses. For subsea cables, it just takes a seafarer dropping and dragging the boat’s anchor.

Russia’s intent is viewed as attempting to disrupt support for Ukraine and cause chaos in Europe, including financial losses, fueling divisions in society and trust in authorities.

“If you can do that at very small expense, and with not very much effort, and with impunity, then if you’re a country like Russia that doesn’t care about its standing in the world, doesn’t care about ethics, morals, or its reputation, then that is clearly a very attractive option,” she said.

The Trump administration is preparing for a three-way meeting between the U.S., Ukraine and Russia for negotiations to end the war, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Friday.

“We are waiting for the United States to propose a date. The United States proposed the United Arab Emirates as the venue for such a meeting,” he said.

Meanwhile, Zelensky said Ukraine is offering to help Europe better defend against Russia’s hybrid warfare, specifically in defending against drone incursions. German authorities have blamed Russia for carrying out a foiled drone attack against Leipzig/Halle Airport in August.

The Danish intelligence report warned that there is a low, but growing risk Russia could launch a limited military attack using long-range weapons on critical infrastructure, or a false-flag operation using a Ukrainian-made drone to attack a NATO country.

“Russia’s behavior, their choice, is to continue escalating,” Zelensky said.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy attorney Kevin Reddington fires back at lone holdout juror's attorney after fiery interview
articles.summary: Kevin Reddington fires back at Edward Paltzik, calling the holdout juror's attorney a "histrionic individual" as Lindsay Clancy's defense fights on.

"I think Ed ought to learn how to go into the courtroom and articulate his position rather than be a histrionic individual that's just mouthing off for the media," Reddington told Fox News Digital. "It's all based on sound, law, facts, jury questions, and I'm doing what I should do, representing Lindsay. And I'm pretty sure that Ed would have probably done the same thing, were it in Houston, and he was representing his client." In an interview with Ray Marcel, a YouTuber who streams under the pseudonym FugitiveTV, Paltzik also called for Clancy's execution, although she hasn't been convicted of any criminal charges and Massachusetts does not impose the death penalty. LINDSAY CLANCY HOLDOUT JUROR MAKES NEW PROMISE AS LAWYER WARNS OF PUBLIC ATTACKS "Ed, why don't you just shut up?" Reddington said. "Really, you foul individual." However, Reddington joked that he didn't get Paltzik's "Shooter McGavin" reference at first but agreed that it was a funny jab after having someone explain it to him. Paltzik fired back on Friday. "It’s really not complicated. I’m not backing down. I’m not backing off of it one inch. It should not be controversial at all that I called Lindsay Clancy a ‘demon.’ …She strangled her three innocent children," he told Fox News Digital. And as for the challenge from Reddington to see him in court, he said he's working to find local counsel and that filings would be coming. "Kevin Reddington was doing his job but the problem is it’s off the rails now," Paltzik continued. "I’m speaking as a criminal defense attorney for almost 20 years. I would never criticize a juror. And I would never file a post-trial motion to investigate the juror." FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X Reddington also took issue with the juror being described as the "lone holdout juror." articles.title: Israeli minister Bezalel Smotrich calls for war in occupied West Bank
articles.summary: Comments come as Israeli authorities announce military closure across occupied West Bank, citing Jewish holiday Sukkot.
articles.body:
Far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich says the Israeli military should “go to war” in the occupied West Bank and repeat what it “did in Gaza”.

Using a biblical term for the occupied West Bank, the minister told Ynet News in an interview published on Sunday that Israel needs to “go to war in Judea and Samaria, to do there what we did in Gaza, to dismantle the Palestinian Authority, which is a terror authority”.

Smotrich was responding to a question on how Israel should combat the increasing “security tensions” in the occupied West Bank, where Israeli violence against Palestinians has been steadily growing since the eruption of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023, but the attacks have intensified significantly this year.

“We need to tell” Israeli forces, he said, “Just as you dismantled Hamas in Gaza, there won’t be terror infrastructure in Judea and Samaria”. “No terrorists, no weapons, no tunnels.”

The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) recorded more than 1,330 settler-related attacks on Palestinians in the West Bank from January to late July, averaging six a day, the highest rate in about 20 years.

Various settler groups , often supported or protected by Israeli soldiers, have attacked Palestinians in several ways, including shootings, besieging homes and engaging in other forms of communal violence that experts have described as “ pogroms “.

Rights groups warn that settlers are increasingly armed with military-issued weaponry and wear military uniforms during attacks, blurring the line between settler and soldier.

In a statement later on Sunday, the Palestinian Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates said Smotrich’s comments come within the context of Israeli government policies that involve the killing and displacement of Palestinians, as well the expansion of illegal settlements, land confiscation and attempts to impose annexation by force.

It also warned that continued international silence over inflammatory Israeli statements and policies encourages the Israeli government to pursue its plans and risks further regionall tension and instability.

The comments come as Israeli authorities announced a comprehensive military closure across the occupied West Bank, citing the Jewish holiday of Sukkot. The heightened restrictions on the movement of Palestinians are set to remain in place until October 3.

Meanwhile, in occupied East Jerusalem, hundreds of Israelis stormed the courtyards of Al-Aqsa Mosque under heavy protection from Israeli police on Sunday.

Palestinian news agency Wafa reported that the Israelis entered the compound through the Moroccan Gate and performed Talmudic rituals, as Israeli forces increased restrictions around the mosque and across Jerusalem’s Old City.

articles.title: Tensions run high in Northern Ireland after contentious march given go-ahead
articles.summary: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham called for calm in Northern Ireland on Sunday after a contentious parade was given the go-ahead by the High Court in Belfast in a late-night sitting.
articles.body: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham called for calm in Northern Ireland on Sunday after a contentious parade was given the go-ahead by the High Court in Belfast in a late-night sitting. Thousands of protesters, many wearing balaclavas, gathered to block the marchers from the Orange Order, a group hugely supportive of Northern Ireland being part of the UK, from proceeding down a street in the town of Portadown where many favor unification with the Republic of Ireland. Fireworks were set off nearby about five minutes before its 8 a.m. start time, and protesters were notified on a loudspeaker that they will be liable for arrest for taking part in an unlicensed counter parade. Burnham appealed for “calm on all sides” over the parade, saying there have been “big gains made in Northern Ireland, and we don’t want to see things go backwards.” Sunday’s march marks the first time in almost 30 years that an Orange Order parade has been allowed to go down Garvaghy Road. The road was a notorious flashpoint before the Good Friday Agreement of 1998 largely ended bloodshed that left 3,600 people dead, some 50,000 wounded and thousands bereaved. In the years before the agreement, there were violent clashes on Garvaghy Road over several summers and requiring major security operations. Ending the Troubles meant balancing competing identities in Northern Ireland, which remained in the United Kingdom when the rest of Ireland won independence a century ago. Irish nationalists in the north — most of them Catholic — seek union with the Republic of Ireland, while largely Protestant unionists want to stay part of the UK. Mary Lou McDonald, the president of Sinn Fein, the party historically linked to the Irish Republican Army, said the people of Garvaghy Road would “not be drawn back to the past.” “This is madness,” she said. “This, in fact, is primitive treatment of any community in the year 2026. It is intolerable, and it will not be tolerated.” Gavin Robinson, the leader of the Democrat Unionist Party, the largest pro-U.K. party in Northern Ireland, called out Sinn Fein leaders for inflaming the situation. “The rule of law cannot apply only when Sinn Fein likes the outcome,” he said. “Our institutions are founded on respect for the police, the courts and the rule of law.” The march was given the final go-ahead at a court hearing which concluded at 2.15 a.m. Sunday.

images.caption: People block the Garvaghy road, a Catholic enclave in the largely Protestant town of Portadown, on the day members of the Protestant Orange Order are expected to march through the area as they take part in the annual Drumcree parade, Northern Ireland, on September 27, 2026.

articles.title: ‘My hands are empty’: Displaced Palestinians struggle to survive
articles.summary: In Tulkarem and other West Bank cities, displaced Palestinians are being forced deeper into debt and poverty.
articles.body:
Tulkarem, occupied West Bank – Hakim Mar’i spends his days lying on a single bed, his disfigured leg raised. The windows of Mar’i’s dilapidated apartment, his latest temporary shelter, are covered with old blankets. Unable to work, Mar’i has no money for electricity, so the blankets have to do. At night, his family lives in near darkness.

The apartment is just around the corner from mounds of rubble and gnarled iron structures that mark one entrance to the now-emptied Tulkarem refugee camp. For Mar’i and other Palestinians, the camp was a home once considered temporary. But generations lived there, and now, the physical structure – their home – that tied his family together over the years is gone.

Impoverished, Hakim’s family is in disarray. With its debts mounting and its members facing another eviction, he said he has considered taking his life several times over the past year and a half.

Mar’i cannot afford treatment for his debilitating leg injury, which has developed severe infections. He said he sustained it while working as a labourer inside Israel in 2019. The wound worsened after Israeli soldiers severely beat him when they forced his family from the Tulkarem camp. Diabetes and other untreated conditions have piled on, but he is unable to pay for the needed medical care.

“This joint here is completely gone,” he said, gesturing at the swollen, blackened lower leg that prevents him from working.

“The medicine – by God, the medicine, I haven’t been able to get. My wife and kids tell me: get out travel. Go to America, Turkey – so I can the medical treatment I need… I’m a sick man.”

His mother, Salwa, sat beside him, less than a kilometre (0.6 miles) from their former four-storey home. She wept when asked about the family home that was built floor by floor after they were first displaced in 1948 from al-Khudayra, the Arabic name for Hadera, a city in Israel. “We really put a lot into that house,” she said.

After their removal, the Israeli military razed the Mar’i home so a road traversing the now-emptied camp could be built. “Seeing it destroyed was really painful for us – all of us,” she said.

It has been more than 20 months since Israeli forces emptied the Jenin, Tulkarem and Nur Shams refugee camps in a sweeping military operation in the northern West Bank, displacing tens of thousands of Palestinians whose families had already been refugees for three generations. Constantly renewed orders for a closed military zone now prevent their return.

Since January 2025, Hakim’s family has been forced to move four times. First, they fled to a converted youth centre before landing in a cramped apartment with their four children, all under 15.

Unable to pay rent, the family could see the landlord’s generosity run its course as this once-temporary housing arrangement now has no end in sight. Hakim owes money at the local shops for food he bought on credit. Some nights, the children eat at neighbours’ houses.

“I have children. I have food. I have drink,” he said. “My hands are empty. Nobody is with me. Nobody is standing beside me.”

The Mar’i family is among more than 33,000 Palestinians forcibly removed from the Jenin, Nur Shams and Tulkarem camps by Israeli forces in early 2025. This is the largest single episode of forced displacement in the West Bank since Israel’s occupation began in 1967, according to the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA).

UN satellite imagery shows that 20 percent of all buildings across the three camps have been destroyed and another 28 percent are damaged.

“The level of destruction we are seeing is severe and unprecedented,” said Roland Friedrich, director of West Bank affairs for the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, UNRWA.

According to Friedrich, 85 percent of those displaced have no regular income after many lost jobs when the camps were emptied. More than 80 percent of residents are renting, an unfamiliar expense for families who never paid for housing or utilities inside the camps.

The closed military zone covering the camps is renewed every two months, Friedrich said, with no indication of when – or whether – residents will be allowed to return. “What we saw there is forced displacement,” Friedrich said. “The UN’s position is very clear: People have to be allowed to return. The camps must be rebuilt.”

Unlike after the 2000-2005 second Intifada when the Jenin camp was rebuilt, displaced families and UNRWA staff fear there is no return plan this time.

The Israeli military stated the camps were emptied for “operational security” in its effort to root out fighters from the camps. Friedrich worried the aim of the military operations is to “change the geographical expression of the Palestinian refugee issue”.

Now more than 20 months into what was meant to be an emergency response, funding shortages have left UNRWA unable to cover the vast needs of the displaced population. It has moved some operations to keep schools and basic health clinics functioning. With funds dwindling, the agency has shifted to a “targeted approach”, leaving thousands without support.

Friedrich pointed to a rise in gender-based violence linked to the economic strain on families and to growing depression and anxiety among displaced children observed by UNRWA’s psychosocial teams. “We’re already at the brink now,” he declared.

While Hakim’s displacement plays out in the shadow of the camp, the family of Khadija Zbeidat face their own imminent eviction on the outskirts of Tulkarem. They live in the neighbourhood of Dhinnaba, where sparse houses are interspersed with greenhouses. They are unable to afford a residence closer to the city centre.

As Khadija sat on a couch in the middle of the yard, her many children and grandchildren ran past a small patch of plants she has planted – one of her few remaining joys. “I love plants,” she said. “We had many flowers in our home in the camp. Having the plants here is all I have to feel like myself,” she told Al Jazeera.

Khadija, a widow, shares a tiny spartan room with nine family members, nearly all children, along with a small bathroom and a kitchen barely big enough for one person to cook in. A worn couch takes up one corner. The ceiling is peeling above it.

The room was given to them rent free by a relative of Khadija’s brother-in-law after they spent four months crammed into her daughter’s house with nine other people. “It got really cramped, the pressure on each other,” Zbeidat said. “And we became a burden too.”

Khadija’s family was displaced in January 2025 from the Tulkarem camp’s Haret al-Nadi section, a significant part of which has been destroyed, she said.

“The camp was excellent,” she said of their life before. “I swear, I wish they’d take us back. Everything was close to us, dear – … the closeness, that sense of belonging and the warmth, the company and the neighbours.”

The memories that she cherishes most dearly and that bring her to tears are of food: the stuffed grape leaves and the maamoul cookies made as a neighbourhood together for Eid. This year, there was none of it.

“Nothing. No cookies,” she said. “Nobody even had it in them to do anything any more. Everyone went their own way – scattered.”

Like the Mar’i family and others, they were not allowed to bring their belongings during their abrupt displacement. Some residents have since been allowed to retrieve belongings once or twice from their homes in the camps, but much of what they own remains left behind. Khadija’s daughter-in-law at one point returned to the ruins of the camp – at the risk of being shot – to retrieve a doll left behind that Khadija’s granddaughter Sandy would not stop crying about.

In Tulkarem, displaced families live either in the poorest areas closest to the camp, like the Mar’is, or on the cheaper outskirts, like the Zbeidats, remaining close enough to the health and schooling services that UNRWA still provides. But even a simple trip to buy groceries requires Khadija, who has no car, to travel 2km (1.2 miles).

At night, the family sits outside rather than in the stifling heat of the poorly ventilated room, watching Israeli military drones pass low overhead. “What to do? We’re used to seeing them, to having them around, to them raiding houses,” Khadija said. “It doesn’t matter any more.”

The military raids that always haunted life in the refugee camps have now come to wherever the displaced refugees have fled to. “We don’t feel safe,” Khadija said. “Nor the kids. It’s dangerous. When they want to go out somewhere, my heart stays busy until they come back.”

For months after the displacement, landlords, relatives and shopkeepers absorbed much of the shock, allowing families to stay for free or buy food on credit. But as the emergency stretches to almost two years now, that informal safety net is fraying. The pressure is felt particularly in economically moribund Tulkarem, where many families had relied on jobs inside Israel before Palestinian work permits were revoked after the Hamas-led attacks in southern Israel and the start of Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza in October 2023.

The owner of the property where Khadija’s family is staying recently sent his sister to tell Khadija’s family to leave. “They think it’s been too long,” Khadija explained. “They want the land, to benefit from the land and the room. … But where can we get money, where to pay from? The rent is very high, and we can’t afford it. We don’t know what to do if she comes again and kicks us out.”

Hakim’s family is on the brink of eviction too. Like others, he received from UNRWA a one-time rental subsidy of 3,000 shekels ($985) and a separate 1,700-shekel ($560) multipurpose cash payment for short-term assistance. “Every minute, I am waiting for the landlord to kick us out,” he said.

Khadija’s family survives on credit from shopkeepers who know their situation and, for now, still extend it – but patience is wearing thin.

Hakim said this goodwill is collapsing: “You tell them: ‘Give me a day, two days. Be patient with me.’ They won’t bear it.”

As distant as a return to her family’s lands in 1948 feels now, Khadija still hopes to return to the camp one day. But she worries that her children may inherit an even more precarious existence than the one that preceded this latest dispossession – refugees for generations displaced yet again. “Only God knows what tomorrow will bring us,” Khadija said.

articles.title: Bowes Museum's new art display pays 'homage' to French founder
articles.summary: About 60 impressionist paintings from the UK and France are being shown together in Barnard Castle.
articles.body:
A County Durham museum is paying "homage" to its French founder's routes by bringing in works she would have approved of for its newest exhibition.

The Bowes Museum in Barnard Castle has linked up with a museum in Le Havre for Impressions of Light, featuring a number of impressionist paintings never before been seen in the UK.

The display also highlights the links between the museum's founders, John Bowes and his Parisian wife Josephine , and the French art world.

The museum said the exhibition, which will run until 14 March, involved a detailed planning operation to secure all necessary permissions and logistical arrangements, with specialist art couriers transporting the works.

The exhibition brings together 60 works from Bowes' collection and the Musée d'Art Moderne André Malraux (MuMa), in Le Havre.

Bowes Museum's executive director Hannah Fox said: "It doesn't simply create a dialogue between our two museums, it restores a connection between two worlds.

"While the paintings were made in Normandy, many of the landscapes they depict find unexpected echoes in County Durham."

Fox said the exhibition paid "homage" to Josephine Bowes and her "mold-breaking artistic patronage", uniting the works she collected with "avant-garde" pieces she might have acquired had she lived beyond 1874.

Michaël Debris, assistant curator at MuMa, said: "The collaboration between our two museums has its roots in a longer history."

One of the artworks, Fécamp, Seaside by Claude Monet, is going on display 22 years after the Bowes Museum first requested it.

"As the painting was involved in another project at the time it could not be loaned then, but now it has finally happened," Debris said.

Organisers have spent two and half years planning the exhibition, from discussing its "concept and narrative" through to selecting and securing artworks.

Getting all necessary permissions and logistical arrangements for transportation took just under a year.

Vicky Sturrs, director of programmes and collections at the Bowes Museum, said: "For international loans, artworks are carefully inspected and packed in specialist crates, then transported with specialist art couriers.

"Customs and import requirements are managed alongside detailed documentation, including condition reports and insurance.

"When the artworks arrive, they are carefully unpacked and condition checked again to identify any impact from their journey before they are installed in the gallery space."
