articles.title: ‘No role for UNRWA in Gaza’: Does the Board of Peace toe Israeli lines?
articles.summary: Board of Peace excludes UNRWA from Gaza, aligning with repeated Israeli calls to sideline the refugee aid agency.
articles.body:
The United States-led Board of Peace (BoP) has said the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA) will have no role in Gaza – echoing a longstanding Israeli demand to sideline the organisation considered a lifeline for millions of Palestinians.

The board, which has been tasked with overseeing the “ceasefire” and Gaza’s reconstruction, said on Friday it would work only with partners it deems reliable and who it believes can meet the needs of Gaza’s population – a standard it says UNRWA does not meet.

The move comes as the BoP unveiled a multibillion-dollar plan on Wednesday aimed at beginning Gaza’s reconstruction, nearly a year after a so-called “ceasefire” came into effect in the devastated Palestinian territory.

The plan, presented on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly (UNGA), comes as key elements of the “ceasefire” remain stalled, including the withdrawal of Israeli forces and the disarmament of Hamas.

UNRWA was established in 1949 to cater to tens of thousands of Palestinians displaced from their homes by Jewish militias from areas that currently form part of Israel.

BoP’s stance on UNRWA comes as Israel’s genocide in the coastal enclave continues, with Palestinians facing nonstop attacks, severe restrictions on humanitarian aid and stalled reconstruction plans.

“Excluding UNRWA is not a neutral administrative decision; it is a deeply political one,” Palestinian political analyst and playwright Ahmed Najar told Al Jazeera.

“It aligns the Board of Peace with Israel’s longstanding campaign to marginalise and ultimately dismantle the agency, removing it not only from Gaza’s present but from its future.”

So what has BoP said about UNRWA, and does it keep toeing the Israeli line on the future of Gaza?

The BoP unveiled a 66-project reconstruction blueprint on the sidelines of the UNGA, with $2.4bn proposed for projects aimed at beginning Gaza’s recovery.

UNRWA was left off the list of UN agencies the board identified as partners.

“The Board of Peace’s policy as it relates to UNRWA’s involvement in Gaza is unchanged,” the BoP said in a post on X on Friday.

“We will only work with trusted partners who will deliver for the people of Gaza and contribute to a deradicalised Strip. UNRWA fails on those litmus tests.”

However, a BoP official, speaking to The Associated Press news agency on condition of anonymity, confirmed that board members had met UNRWA officials several times.

The official said the agency’s programmes could continue if they served Gaza’s residents well, but maintained that “UNRWA’s days are over”.

The BoP, which US President Donald Trump launched earlier this year, was conceived to oversee the rebuilding of Gaza after nearly three years of Israel’s genocidal war on the Strip.

In an indirect response, UNRWA acting Commissioner-General Christian Saunders said on Friday in Gaza, “UNRWA remains an institution of considerable humanitarian and strategic value, with capabilities and expertise that are difficult to replicate today.”

“To disregard these capabilities at a moment of such profound need is neither logical nor responsible,” Saunders said in a statement.

Former UNRWA chief Philippe Lazzarini on Thursday warned that removing the agency would have a “devastating” effect on Palestinians.

“They want to get rid of the agency, but on the other hand they know that if you get completely rid of the agency today, it might have a further … devastating impact on the population,” Lazzarini told AP on Friday.

In a separate statement on X, Lazzarini said, “grandiose plans are what the Board of Peace does best”, noting widespread suffering across Gaza amid Israel’s ongoing genocide.

The agency has about 11,000 Palestinian employees in Gaza and remains heavily involved in healthcare, education, water and sanitation services. Its exclusion is particularly significant given the scale of displacement and the continuing restrictions on aid entering Gaza.

UNRWA has for decades provided aid and education services to Palestinians in Gaza, occupied East Jerusalem and the West Bank as well as Jordan, Syria and Lebanon – the neighbouring countries where the Palestinian refugees have been living.

Palestinians see the agency as safeguarding their right of return to their homeland, while Israel wants it dismantled.

Hamas accused the BoP of adopting Israel’s position.

Spokesperson Hazem Qassem on Saturday called the decision to exclude UNRWA “a complete alignment with the Zionist [Israeli] position”, saying it was aimed at ending the agency’s operations, preventing it from delivering aid and undermining Palestinian refugees’ right of return.

Qassem said it was “strange for the peace council to adopt this hostile stance towards UNRWA while simultaneously failing to provide aid to Gaza or compel the occupation to abide by the ceasefire agreement and halt the daily killings of Palestinians in the Strip”.

Does the Board of Peace toe the Israeli line?

Experts say the workings and demands of the BoP align closely with Israel’s vision of the Gaza Strip and the Palestinians.

“The composition of the board reinforces this concern,” analyst Najar told Al Jazeera,” he said.

“Israel is a founding member, while Palestine is not. Not a single Palestinian sits on either the central executive board or the Gaza executive board. Yet these bodies include senior Trump officials, strongly pro-Israel figures, private-equity executives and Israeli businesspeople who will exercise influence over Gaza’s governance and reconstruction.”

Nevertheless, Najar said, while other members such as Turkiye may “provide some counterweight”, so the board does not present itself to be “entirely uniform”, the structure of power is “clear”.

“Palestinians are excluded from the bodies taking the strategic, financial and security decisions about their own land,” he added.

Israel has for years sought to remove UNRWA from Gaza, accusing the agency of being infiltrated by Hamas.

The International Court of Justice, in an advisory opinion in October, said allegations that “a significant part of UNRWA’s employees are ‘members of Hamas … or other terrorist factions'” had not been substantiated.

The BoP’s position strengthens the Israeli efforts to dismantle the UN agency.

Najar said Israel’s “hostility” towards the UN agency is also connected to what the agency represents: “the continuing existence of Palestinian refugees, their rights – including their right of return – and the international community’s unresolved responsibility towards them”.

“Removing UNRWA, therefore, serves a political purpose extending far beyond the delivery of aid,” he added.

Najar said Gaza could not be “credibly reconstructed” by excluding the UN agency. “Nor should reconstruction be used to erase Palestinian refugee rights or replace an internationally mandated institution with mechanisms that are more politically compliant. If the board is serious about rebuilding Gaza for its people, UNRWA must be part of that process, and Palestinians must be at its centre, not placed at the bottom of a foreign-controlled hierarchy,” he noted.

Hamas and other Palestinian factions agreed in July to a roadmap under which weapons would be surrendered in stages as Israeli forces gradually withdrew. The two processes were explicitly linked.

But following an August meeting between Nickolay Mladenov, the BoP’s director-general, and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the board said Israeli forces would not withdraw beyond the “Yellow Line” until Hamas’s decommissioning was complete, including “light weapons, heavy weapons, and the tunnels alike”.

Hamas maintains that it will not implement its obligations unless Israel fulfils its own.

Israel currently occupies more than 60 percent of Gaza while most of the territory’s 2.3 million people remain displaced.

Article 17 of the BoP plan calls for “temporary reconstruction” beginning in areas designated free of Hamas control, including humanitarian compounds for unarmed civilians.

The proposed system would direct reconstruction, aid and shelter towards areas outside Hamas’s control while Israeli forces remain behind the so-called “Yellow Line”.

However, Israel has refused to allow the Palestinian technocratic committee into Gaza, open crossings or begin reconstruction until Hamas is completely disarmed.

After unveiling the reconstruction plan on the sidelines of the UNGA, BoP high representative Mladenov said once again the proposed plan depends on Hamas’s disarmament.

Almost a year after the October 2025 ceasefire, reconstruction has yet to begin on any meaningful scale and Israeli forces continue to occupy large parts of the Strip.

At least 1,451 Palestinians have been killed and 4,953 wounded in Israeli attacks since the “ceasefire” began in October 2025, according to Gaza’s Ministry of Health.

The healthcare system is on the verge of “total collapse”, the ministry said last week, while shortages of fuel, medical supplies and spare parts have disrupted hospitals, water and sanitation services.

The scale of destruction is also immense. More than half of Gaza’s hospitals and clinics remain nonfunctional, less than 1.5 percent of cropland is accessible and undamaged, and reconstruction needs have reached an estimated $71.5bn.

Nearly 84 percent of Gaza’s population – more than 1.76 million people – are living in displacement sites or damaged and inadequate shelters, the UN has said.

articles.title: Swiss voters set to reject tighter neutrality rules that would curb NATO cooperation
articles.summary: ZURICH — Swiss voters on Sunday looked set to reject a proposal to adopt a more restrictive form of neutrality that ⁠would have blocked their country from imposing economic sanctions or cooperating with NATO.
articles.body: ZURICH — Swiss voters on Sunday looked set to reject a proposal to adopt a more restrictive form of neutrality that ⁠would have blocked their country from imposing economic sanctions or cooperating with NATO. More than two-thirds voted against a proposal for a strictly defined version of neutrality to be written into the Swiss constitution, according to the latest referendum projections by state broadcaster SRF. While Swiss neutrality has been internationally ⁠recognised since the end of the Napoleonic wars in ​1815, ⁠how the government implements it is not spelled out. The right-wing Swiss People’s Party (SVP) has said that Switzerland’s traditional position has been eroded after Bern imposed sanctions ⁠on Russia following its invasion of Ukraine. The campaign has funded posters across the ​country ⁠urging people to vote “No war, yes ‌to neutrality”, featuring white peace doves ahead of the vote. Still, opinion polls suggest voters will reject the proposal, with one of the latest surveys showing 68% against with 31% ‌in favour. Most parties oppose proposal Fabio Wasserfallen, ‌a professor of European politics at the University of Bern, said: “Swiss voters like neutrality, but they approve of how the government is implementing it at present. “They are also generally in favour of the sanctions on Russia ⁠over the war in Ukraine, and don’t want that to change.” The campaign wants the constitution to stipulate that Switzerland cannot join or cooperate with any military or defence alliance unless attacked, and that it refrain from joining any sanctions unless approved by the United Nations. It says Swiss neutrality has served the country well in the past, keeping it out of both world wars, and also helps Bern offer its ‘good offices’ to help ‌negotiate peace between warring parties. “Switzerland has not had a war for 200 ​years because it is permanently armed and neutral,” said Christoph Blocher, the billionaire businessman ‌and backer of the SVP. “But neutrality ⁠has been followed less and less in recent years,” he told Reuters, ⁠with Russia now seeing Switzerland as a party to the conflict because of the sanctions. Apart from the SVP, ‌most parties and the ​Swiss government oppose the proposal, with Foreign Minister ‌Ignazio Cassis saying it would harm national ​security and prevent Switzerland from training with NATO.

articles.title: 5 arrested near UK’s RAF Fairford in explosives probe, US base on highest alert: Key details
articles.summary: A major incident was declared near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire on Sunday after five men were arrested on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act as
articles.body: A major incident was declared near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire on Sunday after five men were arrested on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act as well as offences under the Explosives Act, prompting the evacuation of homes in the nearby village of Whelford.Assistant chief constable Richard Ocone said police received a call at about 12:45 am (local time) regarding three suspicious vehicles near RAF Fairford. The five men have been taken into custody, and police are working with counterterrorism officers.Police said the situation had been contained, while an Army explosive ordnance disposal team examined several vehicles.Aerial footage from Sky News appeared to show a bomb disposal robot moving between three white trucks, with the rear doors of two vans open and large black items visible nearby.Counter-terrorism police are leading the investigation.Here is what we know so far.What happened?Gloucestershire Police said five men were arrested early on Sunday on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act.They are also being held on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act.Ocone said police received a call at around 12:45 am (local time) about three suspicious vehicles near RAF Fairford. The men were subsequently taken into custody, with counterterrorism police involved in the investigation.A number of properties in Whelford were evacuated and residents were taken to a nearby leisure centre in Cirencester while emergency services dealt with the incident.Ocone said 85 households in Whelford had been evacuated as a precaution. The village backs onto the air base.Police said a cordon had been established and that they believed the situation was contained.“We are working closely with our partners and are enacting the well-rehearsed plans we have in place,” Gloucestershire Police said, as reported by the BBC.A large emergency services presence was reported in the area, including a Hazardous Area Response Team.A local resident, Julian Tudsbery, who has lived in Whelford for 30 years, said a resident had reported seeing three “suspicious vans” in the village in the early hours, according to news agency AP.He said police arrived and residents were told to evacuate because there had been a major incident.Why is RAF Fairford significant?Whelford is near RAF Fairford, a Royal Air Force base that hosts US Air Force personnel.The base hosts the headquarters of the US Air Force's 501st Combat Support Wing and the 420th Air Base Squadron.The base has recently been used by US forces during the conflict with Iran. According to the BBC, four American bombers arrived at RAF Fairford in March after then-prime minister Keir Starmer authorised US action described as “defensive” against Iranian missile sites from UK bases.The UK government allowed the US military to use Fairford to strike Iranian missile sites after the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran on February 28. Iran has said bombers flying from the base have been used for strikes beyond the original remit.Police have not confirmed that Sunday's arrests or the explosives investigation are connected to RAF Fairford, although the proximity of the arrests to the base has raised speculation about a possible connection.The US department of defence raised the threat level at RAF Lakenheath in Suffolk following the incident near Fairford. RAF Lakenheath confirmed it was on Charlie alert, the second-highest threat level issued by the US department of defence.According to the BBC, RAF Fairford had been raised to Delta, the highest threat level.What has the US Air Force said?A US Air Force spokesperson said US and British personnel at RAF Fairford “remain vigilant” and declined to discuss specific force-protection measures for security reasons.“For operational security reasons we will not discuss specific force protection measures,” the spokesperson said. “We constantly assess a variety of factors that determine what measures we institute or modify to protect our installations, our people and their families.”The spokesperson said US and British personnel would take appropriate actions to ensure the safety and security of those at the base.What are officials saying?Defence Secretary Wes Streeting thanked the emergency and specialist teams responding to the incident.“We can be reassured that this is being dealt with,” he said.A government spokesperson also thanked emergency services for acting quickly to detain several suspects and protect the local community, while saying it would be inappropriate to comment further as the investigation continues.Local authorities said the incident was serious, with those living closest to the affected area evacuated to Cirencester Leisure Centre.Prime Minister Andy Burnham is receiving updates on the situation, according to his office.Police have not disclosed the identities of the five men or provided further details about the suspected terrorist act. Authorities have also not confirmed that the arrests or explosives investigation are linked to RAF Fairford.Police are still working to establish what happened at the airbase and in the surrounding area, with counter-terrorism officers leading the investigation.Counter-terrorism police are now leading the investigation, which was in line with normal procedures in similar situations.You use AI every day. articles.summary: For Americans looking to move, the next hot neighbourhood may not be a bustling downtown or a long-established suburb.
articles.body: For Americans looking to move, the next hot neighbourhood may not be a bustling downtown or a long-established suburb. It could be a new community near an airport, where housing construction and jobs are bringing in a steady stream of residents.Aurora, Colorado's 80019 ZIP code, near Denver International Airport, has emerged as the most popular landing spot for movers in the US, according to the September edition of MovingPlace's Hottest ZIP Codes report, as reported by the New York Post.The ranking is based on 890,131 moves recorded in August and measures the number of newcomers a ZIP code attracts relative to its size.Aurora jumped from a tie for eighth place in the previous month's ranking to the top spot.New housing puts Aurora on the mapThe 80019 corridor is part of a relatively new area of Aurora, where master-planned communities including Painted Prairie and High Point have been adding homes.The typical home in the area is valued at $529,300, while the median household income is $129,154.Daniel Cobb, senior editor at MovingPlace, said the strongest moving activity was concentrated in places with substantial new housing construction or a steady flow of people relocating for work.“Aurora is a good example,” Cobb told the New York Post. “The 80019 suburban corridor is still relatively new, with a lot of housing being added around Denver International Airport.”He said lower land costs had helped keep rents and new-home prices relatively affordable compared with other parts of the Denver area.Military moves lift Kansas ZIP to No. 2Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, retained the second spot in the ranking for the second consecutive month.The Army installation on the Missouri River houses the Combined Arms Center and the Command and General Staff College. Its position on the list is linked largely to military relocations rather than people choosing the area as a lifestyle destination, according to Cobb.“Fort Leavenworth is heavily influenced by military moves,” he said, adding that the area's small population means routine movements of service members and their families can have a significant impact on its ranking.Cobb also noted that the effect can become more pronounced after the peak summer moving season, when activity in other locations begins to slow.Florida takes three of the top 10 spotsFlorida featured prominently in the September list, with three ZIP codes making the top 10.Port Saint Lucie's 34987 ranked third, helped by the large Tradition development. The area has attracted retirees and remote workers moving from the Northeast. Homes there have a median value of $430,100.Inlet Beach, a community along Florida's Highway 30A near Rosemary Beach and Alys Beach, ranked fourth. It had the highest median home value among the ZIP codes in the top 10, at $947,700. Its return to the ranking was linked in the report to wealthy buyers purchasing vacation homes.Bradenton's 34211, which includes the growing Lakewood Ranch area east of Sarasota, ranked sixth. New construction has helped drive moving activity there, with homes valued at a median $601,300.Texas, Virginia and other markets make the listTexas had two entries, both in the Dallas-Fort Worth exurbs. Lavon's 75166 ranked fifth, continuing its recent appearances on the list, while Justin's 76247 entered the top 10 at No. 9. The Denton County community has seen developments such as Union Park emerge from former ranchland.Richmond, Virginia's 23230 ranked seventh after leading the national list in July. The renter-heavy West End area is near Willow Lawn.Downtown Hartford, Connecticut's 06103 debuted at No. 8, with office-to-apartment conversions contributing to activity in an area with relatively few full-time residents.Nashville's 37203, covering Midtown and Music Row, ranked 10th, with new rental towers attracting young professionals.Three ZIP codes that featured in the previous month's top 10 — Richmond's 23219, El Paso's 79908 and Nashville's 37228 — dropped out of the latest ranking.The September list highlights how new housing construction, employment-related relocation, military movements and new rental developments are shaping where Americans are moving, according to the report.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.body:
President Trump is slated to attend the final round of the Presidents Cup golf tournament in Chicago Sunday morning, roughly a month after PGA Tour named him the event’s honorary chair.

Trump last attended the competition in 2017 during his first term, where he presented the trophy to the winning team . It is unclear whether he will do the same during this year’s visit, though the USA TODAY Network’s Golfweek reported that he requested to deliver a 15-minute speech at some point during the competition.

The competition, at Chicago’s Medinah Country Club, will begin just after noon EDT.

Over the past week, the president has engaged in several high-stakes meetings with foreign officials, most notably a three-day visit with Chinese President Xi Jinping, as the United Nations General Assembly meeting in New York City continues through Tuesday.

Meanwhile, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is set to appear on CBS News’s “Face the Nation” Sunday morning, a day after Trump rejected Iran’s seven-day proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and enter a ceasefire. Another Islamic Republic official, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, is scheduled for an interview on NBC News’s “Meet the Press.”

A number of Trump administration officials and lawmakers — such as Attorney General Todd Blanche, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) and Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) — are also set for Sunday morning news show appearances.

articles.title: Bill Gates says getting countries to agree on AI regulations will be harder than Cold War-era nuclear negotiations
articles.summary: Bill Gates called on the U.S. to lead in the global regulation of AI growth but warned agreeing on a global AI regulation could be “more difficult” than Cold War-era nuclear negotiations.
articles.body: Microsoft co-founder and billionaire philanthropist Bill Gates called on the U.S. to be a leader in regulating the growth of artificial intelligence but warned that getting countries to agree on a global framework could be “more difficult” than Cold War-era negotiations to limit nuclear weapons. “This is more difficult than that was,” Gates told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” on Wednesday during a wide-ranging discussion on AI that aired Sunday. His remarks came as he spoke about President Donald Trump’s stance against regulating AI. The president earlier this month rejected calls for the federal government to impose guardrails for companies building AI models, saying in a post on Truth Social, “WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS! We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so.” Gates argued Wednesday that regulating AI companies by imposing monitoring systems would not hamper the U.S. in any race with China to develop superior technology. “What he said is fine, but I think after he hears from me and other people, including that this does not handicap us in whatever he thinks the nation-state race is, that, you know, we will come to a consensus,” the tech mogul said. Gates later pointed to other times the U.S. has led the world in coming up with broad agreements to protect humanity. “Since World War II, the U.S. should be very proud that when there have been global challenges, we, in a way that was benign, where we had friends and allies coming along with us, you know, aviation safety, ozone layer, nuclear weapons, a lot of things where we played the fair actor, not aggrandizing whatever our unique strengths were,” he told moderator Kristen Welker. “And AI is one we’re going to have to go back to this, ‘Hey, humanity is all in this together.’” Concerns about AI reached a fever pitch this month after Jacob Coxon, a whistleblower who had recently resigned from Anthropic, issued a public warning: “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” Days later, two of the nation’s leading AI CEOs — Dario Amodei of Anthropic and Sam Altman of OpenAI — agreed there is a need to slow the pace of AI development amid fears the tech would soon be capable of “superintelligence” that outpaces human thinking. In a blog post, Amodei wrote that “frontier” AI companies must slow down the pace of AI development but only to a point where the companies still lead China. He also urged global coordination between democratic and authoritarian governments to create regulations. In recent weeks, both companies have announced plans to track the behavior of AI agents after OpenAI flagged multiple incidents in which its agents behaved in a concerning way, including by hacking an outside company without being told to do so. In a post on Truth Social ahead of a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday, Trump wrote: “Super Intelligence (SI) will be a big topic of discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is. That is China’s position also.” Addressing immediate concerns about AI While many have been calling for regulations that would limit AI from destroying humanity, Gates said on “Meet the Press” that he believes there should be guardrails in place to prevent mass-casualty events that could be coordinated with the help of AI today. “The most dangerous thing we’re facing right now is people with bad intent using AI. You know, so somebody who wants to defraud an individual or wants to shut down the electric network or scramble bank accounts, they are now empowered,” the philanthropist said. “Historically, countries had cyberattack teams and they could think of things like bioterror weapons,” he said. “Now, small groups with AI can do what only the biggest countries could do. So it’s really the bad intent plus AI that looms as a major threat. Unless governments insist on various safeguards, you know, we will see a lot of big, negative things because we’re not safeguarding.” Gates specifically said monitoring, “where you’re watching what the AI is doing,” is an important safeguard to introduce in each AI lab. “Law enforcement is going to get called up on all these fraud events or, you know, transmission shutdown events,” he added. “And their ability to see what’s going on is going to be nil unless the monitoring and safeguards are built into the AI.” Plus, Gates said, these kinds of safety features can be added to current AI systems without slowing down the pace of development. “That’s another debate — of should we slow down or not,” he said. “But deciding to put the safeguards and monitoring in, that’s a choice we have. And the only question is, Do we do that before or after there’s some large-scale cyberattacks or bioattacks?” One bipartisan proposal in Congress would require a “kill switch,” or a way for AI companies to immediately suspend or shut down their AI services if a dangerous situation occurs. Gates said “it’s not enough to have a kill switch” and renewed his calls for internal monitoring and safeguards. “I would never want to say I’m against a kill switch,” he added. “But when you’re trying to moderate the bad behavior, you need insight and records of what’s being done. So the kill switch alone would not prevent these tragedies.” The Gates Foundation and AI The philanthropist, who now leads the Gates Foundation, also spoke about the group’s work expanding AI access to countries where English isn’t the primary language. “AI models have gotten very good at recognizing English and about a dozen other mainstream languages. And so as you talk about your health, it’s going to accurately record that and be able to help you. In African languages, the error rate will be about 10 times higher,” he said, adding that errors can be “very dangerous.” The Gates Foundation, he added, is working with 60 AI companies to expand the reliable languages they offer. “We have a very concrete timeline to improve the quality, to benchmark and then say, ‘OK, this is good enough. You can do a health interview or an education session in this language,’” he added, saying he hopes that within five years every language that a million or more people speak will be close to the quality of English on these platforms. Gates said his foundation is also using AI in its own work. “It’s helping me in the foundation work,” he said. “You know, ‘What’s the latest on malaria? What’s the latest on malnutrition?’ It’s allowing the Gates Foundation, which will spend all its money over the next 19 years — you know, it’s got a bit over $200 billion — that money will be far, far better spent because we’re using AI to guide our work.” A ‘regrettable’ relationship with Jeffrey Epstein In the last year, Gates has also faced scrutiny for his ties to the late Jeffrey Epstein, the disgraced financier and convicted sex offender. When the Justice Department released a trove of files related to Epstein at the direction of federal lawmakers, Gates’ name appeared multiple times, including in emails from Epstein suggesting that Gates had extramarital affairs. The Microsoft co-founder has since called his past relationship with Epstein “foolish” and testified to House lawmakers in June that he did not engage in illegal activity with Epstein. On Wednesday, Gates accused Epstein of using their friendship to boost his reputation. “I was told by Jeffrey after I met him that he could help raise billions of dollars for global health — you know, he wouldn’t be paid, he would have no role. That proved to be a complete dead end. So my spending time with him, like many other people, kind of helped his reputation. You know, that’s very regrettable,” he said.

articles.title: UK police arrest 5 men under terrorism, explosives acts close to US air base
articles.summary: The village of Whelford is located around 2 miles from RAF Fairford.
articles.body:
British police announced on Sunday morning that five people were arrested "on suspicion of offenses under the explosives act" close to a major air base hosting U.S. forces in the southwest of England.

"A number of properties are currently being evacuated in the Whelford area following the declaration of a major incident," Gloucestershire Police said in a statement. "It follows the arrest of several men on suspicion of offenses under the explosives act."

The village of Whelford is located around 2 miles from RAF Fairford, which hosts the U.S. Air Force and has since February been serving as a key hub for American operations against Iran -- including for heavy bombers like the B-1 Lancer and B-52 Stratofortress.

"The Army's specialist explosive ordnance disposal team are currently examining a number of vehicles," the police statement said.

Local residents were evacuated to a nearby recreation center, with a cordon put in place. "We believe this incident is contained," police said. "We are working closely with our partners and are enacting the well-rehearsed plans we have in place."

During a press conference later on Sunday, Assistant Chief Constable Richard Ocone said that police acted after receiving a call about three suspicious vehicles traveling toward the base at 12:45 a.m.

Officers arrested five men, who remain in custody, on suspicion of explosive offenses, Ocone said. Local police, he added, are working closely with counter-terror police on the investigation.

Counter Terrorism Policing confirmed that the five detained men were also arrested "on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act."

Police said that a 400m cordon was put in place around the suspect's vehicles while armed forces explosives experts examine them. Around 85 households were also evacuated as a "precaution," police said.

A British government spokesperson told ABC News that Prime Minister Andy Burnham "is being kept updated on the incident in Gloucestershire."

"We are grateful to the emergency services, who have acted quickly to detain several suspects and put measures in place to keep the community safe," they added. "It would be inappropriate to comment further whilst investigations are ongoing."

British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said in a post to X, "We can be reassured that this is being dealt with, and it is exactly why our emergency response teams and Armed Forces are on standby 24/7."

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood also posted to X thanking the emergency services "for their swift response to the major incident in Gloucestershire this morning and their reassurance that they believe the incident is contained."

A spokesperson for the U.S. Air Force 501st Combat Support Wing, based at RAF Fairford, told ABC News that the unit "appreciates the swift response and continued support of our local law enforcement partners."

"The safety and security of our airmen, families, and surrounding communities remains our highest priority," the spokesperson added. "We remain in close coordination with our U.K. partners to help ensure the safety and security of both our military and local communities."

Amid reports that U.S. air bases in the U.K. had raised their threat levels, the 48th Fighter Wing -- an American unit based at RAF Lakenheath in eastern England -- told ABC News in a statement that it was "unable to discuss specific force protection measures" citing "operational security reasons."

"We constantly assess a variety of factors that determine what measures are implemented or modified. Please be assured that the Tri-Base area (RAF Lakenheath, RAF Mildenhall, and RAF Feltwell) remains vigilant and will take appropriate action to ensure the safety and security of U.S. service members, U.S. and U.K. civilians, contractors, and their families," the statement said.

ABC News' Rashid Haddou-Riffi, Guy Davies, Lama Hasan, Kevin Shalvey and Jamie Dorrington contributed to this report.
